messages.subject: Tidy data: calculating the difference in a measurement between control and treatments
messages.subject_clean: Tidy data: calculating the difference in a measurement between control and treatments
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I have a question that I feel should have a simple answer, but all of my current solutions are overly complicated.

I have a dataframe with one column for treatment (‘control’, ‘a’, ‘b’) and then a couple columns of a measurement (‘height’, ‘width’). There’s also a column for sample ID which is consistent across the treatments (‘1’, ‘2’, ‘3’—all of which appear in all three treatments and have each measurement).

I’d like to calculate the difference between the height in the control treatment and the height in each treatment for each of my samples. In a wide format this would be easy—I’d have separate columns for height.control and height.a, and I would just subtract one from the other and make a new column height.difference. For tidy data, my initial thought was to do something like with(df, height[treatment==‘a’] - height[treatment==‘control’]) but I’m not sure how to incorporate multiple treatments (‘a’ to control and ‘b’ to control). Also this assumes my sample IDs are in consistent order, which they are in this case but a more general approach could also be better. I want to save this output as another column, not additional rows—something like ‘height.difference’ which would be 0 for the control rows and non-zero for the other treatment rows.

input
sample.id <http://sample.id>  treatment  height  width
1                  control               2           3
2                  control               1           1
1                  a                          2          1
2                 a                           2          2
1                  b                         3          3
2                 b                          2          4

desired output
sample.id <http://sample.id>  treatment  height  width  height.diff  width.diff
1                  control               2           3       0            0
2                  control               1           1        0           0
1                  a                          2           1        0           -2
2                 a                           2          2        1            1
1                  b                         3          3         1            0
2                 b                           2          4       1            3

Thanks for your ideas and help! This is such a simple thing that I’m not even sure how to search for examples online.

Chhaya

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chhaya,

In the tidy data paradigm, each row is supposed to correspond to an “observation” — which isn’t a single measurement, but "all values measured on the same unit (like a person, or a day, or a race) across attributes” (https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/dev/articles/tidy-data.html).  But what counts as a single unit depends on your research question, the way you’re analyzing your data, and so on.  This can even be different *within* your analysis.  Data can be tidy for one step of your analysis (say, graphing height vs treatment in ggplot) and "too long” for another step (say, taking differences across treatments).  I think this is a point we don’t talk about enough when we talk about long vs. wide data and functions like spread() or gather().

Okay, setting aside the philosophy, you need to use some tools to make your data wider.  To do this for height and width at the same time, you’ll need to use the new pivot_wider() function (https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/dev/articles/pivot.html).  Since I haven’t switched to that yet, and I only have a couple of minutes to write this email, I’m going to explain how to do it using spread().  But that means doing it separately for height and width.

Here’s what it looks like for height:
> height_diff_df = df %>%
> > select(sample.id <http://sample.id>, treatment, height) %>%
> > spread(key = treatment, value = height) %>%
> > mutate(height.a.diff = a - treatment,
> >     height.b.diff = b - treatment)
> >
Then do it the same way for width.  If you want, put the two data frames back together using a join (e.g., left_join(height_diff_df, weight_diff_df, by = c(’sample.id <http://sample.id>’, ’treatment’)).

Dan
----

Your suspicion that it is simple is correct :) No need for any pivoting / reshaping here. In base R you can do this:

d$height.diff = d$height - d[d$treatment == "control", "height"]

R's vector recycling rules will do the right thing here IF:
1. the data is sorted correctly: d = d[order(d$treatment, d$sample.id <http://sample.id>), ]
2. Each sample.id <http://sample.id> has the same number of treatments

For your example:

d = read.table(header = TRUE, text = "sample.id <http://sample.id>  treatment  height  width
+ 1                  control               2           3
+ 2                  control               1           1
+ 1                  a                          2          1
+ 2                 a                           2          2
+ 1                  b                         3          3
+ 2                 b                          2          4")
> d$height.diff = d$height - d[d$treatment == "control", "height"]
> d$width.diff = d$width - d[d$treatment == "control", "width"]
> d

  sample.id <http://sample.id> treatment height width height.diff width.diff

1         1   control      2     3           0          0
2         2   control      1     1           0          0
3         1         a      2     1           0         -2
4         2         a      2     2           1          1
5         1         b      3     3           1          0
6         2         b      2     4           1          3

Best,
Clark

Did you want to run Rstudio server on your instance?

Otherwise using git on Linux requires nothing special other than
installing git. This will be command line git. Were you looking for a
GUI interface (by default linux machines on the cloud do not have
graphical interfaces, it's all ssh shell access).

On an Ubuntu instance:
sudo apt-get install git

Then you can you clone repos from github:
git clone https://github.com/d-rug/d-rug.github.io.git

A guide to using git command line:
https://docs.gitlab.com/ee/gitlab-basics/start-using-git.html

I use RStudio Desktop (not server) on a linux installation without issue.  As to a github interface, I generally use drag-and-drop on GitHub's web interface, rather than a standalone client, but the following are also available according to my google-fu:

https://www.addictivetips.com/ubuntu-linux-tips/best-github-clients-for-linux/

R studio I installed from the PPA (in /etc/apt/sources.list.d):

     deb http://ppa.launchpad.net/opencpu/rstudio/ubuntu xenial main

(if not using the same version of debian linux, the xenial and ubuntu bits may need to be altered; if using RedHat/CentOS, you'll have to use whatever the equivalent `yum` command is)

You may want to check out the Tools->Version Control menu item once you have RStudio installed...it might suit your needs.  As to AWS, there are many sub-flavors of that...  Are you looking for a google drive-like interface?  I only really have experience with AWS SQS (which is painful), but hopefully the guide that Rich sent might be helpful.

--Matt

P.S. These days you don't have to do `sudo apt-get install` ; `sudo apt install` is enough, as many of the old "apt subdashes" were rolled into the main command and apt-get is just an alias to that.

linux is case-sensitive, which is why `CD` doesn't work.  If you're expecting lowercase `cd` to return your current directory, you'll want to use

     pwd

(print/present working directory) instead. Your prompt is showing your current directory as ~, which is an alias(?) for your home directory. If the username is rstudio, `pwd` will auto-expand the ~ to /home/rstudio  The `cd` command in linux is used to change the directory

if you're not sure where your R project files are located, you can use the locate command like

     locate myFile.R

     locate myProject.Rproj

(you may need to instruct your shell to build the database for locate first - I can't remember off the top of my head how to do that).

an alternative would be something like

     find . -type f -name "myFile.R"

or like Alex has suggested, use RStudio to open the directory a bit more directly.

This novice needs a bit of direction in discovering why my script using the Tidyverse/Dplyr 'distinct' function is suddenly returning multiple of the same as distinct from each other. Complete_SPID_list_23_July_2019 <- master_table_clean %>%

Hi everyone

I know this is not directly related to R, but as R geeks are likely to use LaTeX, I thought I would share this here in case that can help someone!

If you want to write your dissertation in LaTeX and use the package ucdavisthesis <https://ctan.org/pkg/ucdavisthesis?lang=en>, but want to use the nice GUI Lyx, I wrote a corresponding lyx layout for ucdavisthesis <https://github.com/MatthieuStigler/ucdavisthesislyx>. That will help you use all the enhanced graphical features of Lyx while writing in plain TeX and having the UC Davis required formatting.

Best,
Matthieu
